en: In the first section, "Explaining the Object," of the *Zhengjie Shifa* (Correct Explanation of the Ten Dharmas) within the *Yiguanxin Xia* (Lower Part of the Single Contemplation of the Mind), composed by the Śramaṇa Zhànrán of Pílíng during the Táng Dynasty, it is asked:
"The preceding citations from various texts have already extensively clarified the object; why is it that here one should clarify only the contemplating subject?"
Therefore, he again clarifies the inconceivable realm.
In response, it is said:
although the essence was previously demonstrated, it was merely a direct pointing to the mind.
The mind is the foundation of all phenomena;
therefore, its essence is shown to be the mind.
However, its inconceivable characteristics have not yet been explained in detail.
Fearing further that people might be deluded, it is like a craftsman creating objects: there is the capacity [of the creator] and the capacity [of the object], and their similarities differ.
Therefore, the present text uses wondrous contemplation to observe [the mind], causing it to become a wondrous realm.
Only when the object corresponds to principle is it so called;
furthermore, by means of the observed object, the observing subject is revealed.
When the meaning of the wondrous object is established, the wondrous contemplation is thereby founded. For this reason, the object is elucidated once again.
Furthermore, because one must know that the wondrous realm is the foundation of the nine vehicles,
and only by practicing the nine according to this foundation can one become capable of entering the stages,
it is therefore called the "Wondrous Contemplation of the Ten Vehicles."
Within this, first the conceivable is clarified,
followed by the inconceivable.
Regarding the initial section on the conceivable, there are ten meanings and ten intentions.
However, this is for the purpose of manifesting the inconceivable.
Within this, the intention of first clarifying the conceivable is to make the inconceivable easy to understand.
Regarding the phrase "easy to understand":
having already heard that the ten realms are distinct and can be conceptually deliberated upon,
this [text] now demonstrates that these ten realms are identical within a single mind.
Thus, within a single mind, the ten realms can be discerned;
therefore, among those things that are conceivable, one may identify "this is the realm of hell" up to "the realm of the Buddha," yet these remain beyond verbal expression.
The explanation must necessarily follow a sequential order;
the ten realms, each distinct, do not contradict the progression from coarse to subtle.
As for the person mentioned, the commentary notes that this is not what is being used here.
To abandon the conceivable and seek the inconceivable elsewhere is to be far removed from the truth.
It is like the manifestation of the provisional for the sake of the real—the provisional is itself the real-provisional;
the revelation of the real through the opening of the provisional—the real is itself the real-provisional.
Whether they are relative or absolute, sequential or non-sequential, all are likewise so. Therefore,
in the subsequent passages explaining the realm of contemplation (*samsaya-viṣaya*),
it sometimes stops at the nine realms.
At times it reaches the Buddha-dharmadhātu.
While the Buddha-dhātu is truly inconceivable,
it is also said to be conceivable when situated after the nine realms.
In this text, following the section on the realm of conceptual thought, it clarifies the Buddha-realm by stating: "Contemplate these [beings] who can deliver and those who are delivered.
How could ultimate perfection and consummation exceed this?
As for "conceptualization," the meaning is as explained above.
Regarding "conceivable phenomena," the following clarifies the basis for such conceptualization:
both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools maintain that all things arise from the mind.
Because of the authority of the teaching, it does not say that the mind is inherently complete.
Whether as six or ten, these all belong to the realm of conceptual thought (*cintya*).
The subsequent section, "If one contemplates," correctly clarifies the characteristics of such conceptual thought.
Within the Buddha-dharmadhātu,
both the one who can deliver and the one who is delivered are all the true mark (lakṣaṇa),
because there is nothing that is not the dharmadhātu, for it is utterly quiescent and undifferentiated.
Who is good and who is evil?
The three virtues and three evils within the preceding realm are obliterated.
Who exists and who does not exist?
When the three previous modes of existence and the non-existence of the two vehicles are obliterated,
who is there to be saved or not saved?
When the three previous teachings and the subject-object duality of the four great vows are obliterated, [what remains?]
Although all phenomena are extinguished, their sequential order remains vividly clear;
yet, if one abandons contemplative reflection,
know that such a person loses both dharmas.
Thus, the general meaning consists of five summaries; the explanation of names has four sections;
the manifestation of the essence has four categories; the inclusion of phenomena has six meanings;
and the partial and complete [teachings] have five gates, both sequential and non-sequential.
The mind is likewise so;
by grasping those [objects] to give rise to understanding and thereby guiding skillful means,
one then accomplishes the present tenfold sublime contemplation.
The nine objects below likewise shift this contemplation to observe those various objects;
it is like the agada medicine that universally cures all ailments.

they are said to be "subsumed.

From "inconceivable" (*acintya*) onwards, the text correctly elucidates the inconceivable realm; though the phrasing differs, the meaning is one.
The intent is neither identity nor difference.
This is because the Dharma of the Three Truths does not emerge apart from cultivation and nature, nor from self and other.
Among these, the initial citation from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* reiterates the previously cited passage concerning the manifestation of the objective realm.
What was previously stated— that "the mind creates" is precisely that "the mind possesses"—
is why the passage concerning creation is cited to prove that the mind possesses [all phenomena].
This is found in the eighteenth fascicle of that sutra.
The Bodhisattva Tathāgatarakṣita spoke in verse:
"The mind is like a skilled painter, creating the various five aggregates within all worlds."
There is nothing that is not created by the Dharma.
As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha;
as it is with the Buddha, so it is with sentient beings.
The mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—
these three are without distinction.
If anyone wishes to seek knowledge of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should contemplate in this manner.
"The mind creates all Tathāgatas.
I do not understand this current passage;
how can it be reconciled with the verse stating that "the mind creates all [phenomena], which are undifferentiated in the three [natures]?"
The statement that "the mind creates" does not go beyond two meanings:
first, from the perspective of principle (*li*), creating is identical to possessing;
second, from the perspective of phenomena (*shi*), it does not transcend the three periods of time.
The three times are further divided into three.

First, that which was created in the past produces results in the present; and that which was created in the past and present produces results in the future—such as [the karma] from beginningless time and that of the present.
Even down to the creation of all karma throughout the limits of the future,
it does not transcend the ten realms, the hundred realms, the thousand suchnesses, and the three thousandfold world system.
Second, that which is created in the present within the present.
This is precisely what is induced by common karma in the present.
The transformation of the mind as it pursues objects is termed "creating.
Because the mind exists, all things exist.
Because the mind is empty, all things are empty.
It is like how a single official may perceive different things as fear, love, intimacy, or enmity.
Third, that which is created through the transformations of the sages also causes sentient beings to transform their minds so that they perceive it;
both cases arise from the inherent principle (li-jù) before there can be any phenomenal function (shi-yòng).
Now, in wishing to cultivate contemplation, one should contemplate only the inherent nature (li-jù).
Both that which is simultaneously negated and that which is simultaneously established are the Dharma-realm;
they spontaneously encompass all that is manifested through the provisional and the real.
As cited in the preceding scripture,
although there are various [categories], they do not exceed the ten realms, the three worlds, and so forth.
Regarding the "Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*), the following explains the meaning of the name "Dharma-realm."
Question:
What is the distinction between the names and meanings of "dharma-dhātu" (the realm of phenomena) and "dharma-tā" (the nature of phenomena)? Answer:
The names differ and the meanings differ, yet the essence is one.
Regarding the term "dharmadhātu":
"dharma" refers to all phenomena (dharmas).
"Realm" (*dhātu*) refers to a constituent part,
because their characteristics are distinct.
All phenomena have the three truths as their constituent parts.
In order to clarify the three truths, ten [syllables] must be added to manifest their characteristics;
thus, the various combinations and permutations of these three characters are explained so as to fully constitute the three truths.
That which is called "dharma-nature" (dharmatā) refers to the fact that all dharmas possess the nature of the three truths.
This nature is also the essential constituent (dharmatva), which cannot be altered;
thus, the nature of the three truths is darkly unified (mysterious), remaining unchanged from beginning to end.
Furthermore, the dharmas of the realms and the dharma-nature are themselves the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
The essence of this true mark is fully endowed with the three truths;
therefore, these three characters are now explained in this text.
First, an explanation is provided based on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*):
the ten numbers are conventional designations (*prajñapti*),
while their basis is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Because one is able to realize that these ten dharmas are all empty,
these ten take the dharma of emptiness as their realm; therefore,
they are called the "ten dharma-realms" (daśa-dharmadhātu).
From this point on, the following section provides an analysis based on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) through the method of distinguishing between separate categories.
The differentiation of the ten phenomena is termed "realms" (*dhātu*).
Therefore, because each of these ten phenomena possesses its own distinct domain, they are called the "ten dharma-realms" (*daśa-dharmadhātu*).
From this point onward, the following section explains the ten dharmas by way of the Middle Way as the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
Since these ten dharmas are none other than the true suchness of the Dharma-realm,
they are called the "ten dharma-realms."
If one reads the three characters "ten dharma-realms" (shí fǎjiè) herein,
they form a phrase according to their meaning;
in the first instance, the ten characters are pronounced separately.
The characters for *dharmadhātu* are pronounced together;
next, the ten characters for *dharma* are pronounced together,
and the character for *dhātu* is pronounced alone.
In the subsequent section, the three characters for the "ten dharma realms" are to be pronounced as a single unit.
By reading the text according to this method and reflecting upon the words,
the meaning of the Three Truths will become manifest.
The three truths are formless and both are invisible;
yet, by means of conventional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*), they can be distinguished through things.
These very conventional phenomena are themselves emptiness and themselves the Middle Way.
Within emptiness, there are two aspects and yet no duality.
The immovability of the nature of mind is provisionally designated by the name "Middle," and the total dissolution of the three thousand realms is provisionally designated by the title "Emptiness."
Although they have perished, they exist as provisional designations established by conventional names.
Following the ten dharma realms, the next section explains the characteristics of the phenomena subsumed within the objects of cognition.
First, the three kinds of worlds are clarified.
Next, it is explained that each and every world possesses the ten suchnesses.
The three worlds are simply the five aggregates of the ten realms as substantial dharmas,
along with the provisional designations of sentient beings and their supporting lands.
Within this, first the world of the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) is explained.
Initially, ten types of the five aggregates are enumerated;
subsequently, in the commentary, one treatise and two sūtras are cited.
This explains the meaning of the Buddha’s dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) as possessing the five aggregates (pañca-skandha).
First, it cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
intending to say:
Nirvāṇa is the unsurpassed five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Next, citing the *Anantārthika-sūtra*, he explains and establishes this in the *Mahā-śāstra*.
How is it known that Nirvāṇa is still called the unsurpassed five aggregates?
When the sutra speaks of "non-existence," it does not mean absolute non-existence;
one should know through verification that it merely refers to the absence of the nine realms of the aggregates (*skandha*).
Next, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* is cited to explain the meaning of "immeasurability."
How can it be known that Nirvāṇa is called an aggregate (skandha)?
Since the Mahāyāna Sūtra states that "form is permanent" and "feeling, perception,
and so forth are permanent," one should know that Nirvāṇa is simply the absence of the nine realms of impermanent aggregates.
Just as in the *Abhidharmakośa*, both the aggregates (*skandha*) and the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*) are called "aggregates," so it is here as well:
both the permanent and the impermanent are collectively termed "aggregates" (*āyatana*).
"Grasping the five aggregates" is followed by the next section, which explains the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*).

Just as grasping the five fingers is conventionally designated as a "fist," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Great Treatise) subsequently cites a treatise to prove that the Buddha-realm (*buddhadhātu*) is also called "sentient beings."
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* (Dà jīng) provides further scriptural proof for this distinction:
it states that there are thirty-four types of internal and external forms, each differing according to their temporal conditions.
Regarding the internal form being different:
first, it is different at the stage of the kalala;
second, it is different at the stage of the arbuda.
Third, they differ at the time of closing the hands;
fourth, they differ at the time of forming blisters;
fifth, they differ at the time of initial birth.
Sixth, there is difference during infancy;
seventh, there is difference during childhood;
eighth, there is difference during youth.
Ninth, the stage of prime is different;
tenth, the stage of old age and death is different.
External forms are likewise so.
The stages of the tooth, stem, branch, leaf, flower, and fruit differ;
therefore, these differences are used to explain the world.
Following the ten types of inhabited realms, the following explains the world of the physical environment (*bhājanaloka*).
First, the four lands are listed as the abodes of sentient beings within the ten realms and the five aggregates (*skandha*).
Next, the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (or *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*) is cited to prove that the Buddha also has an abode, which is likewise called a "land.
Of the preceding nine realms, they are termed "aggregates" and "beings."
The existence of a dwelling land (*bhūmi*) is beyond doubt.
Fearing that one might not believe that even what is called a "name" (*nāman*) or a "birth" (*jāti*) still possesses a dwelling land,
I have therefore cited only the three meanings of the Buddha-realm (*buddha-dhātu*) as proof.
This concludes the thirty types [of phenomena] as being derived from the mind.
Question:
Within the inconceivable, why are only the four noble ones explained?
What phenomena are not included?
Why must the phenomena of the six realms of existence be clearly explained? Answer:
The provisional teachings are derived from the ultimate reality;
since one now wishes to demonstrate that reality, how could one not discuss it?
Generally speaking, within a single cycle of transformation, there are five intended meanings in this exposition.
First, it is to show the path for humans and devas;
second, it is to cause [beings] to weary of saṃsāra;
third, it is to know the objective characteristics of the Bodhisattva’s own vow and compassion for others.
The fourth is for the purpose of knowing the dharmas subsumed within the inconceivable realm;
the fifth is for the desire to cause one to know that the dharma-gate of the inherent evil of nature is universal.
The present text pertains precisely to the fourth and fifth [purposes].
The second and third [worlds] are employed concurrently.
Question:
Upon what scriptural gate (śāstra-mukha) is the establishment of the three worlds based? Answer: [As follows].
According to the commentary on the *Mahā-śāstra* regarding the one hundred and eight samādhis,
it says that upon reaching the explanation of the "Samādhi that Illuminates All Worlds," it states:
"Because one attains this samādhi, one is able to illuminate the three kinds of worlds."
This refers to the world of sentient beings, the world of dwelling places, and the world of the five aggregates.
It continues until the explanation of the "Samādhi that Liberates All Dwelling Places," which states:
"One who attains this samādhi..."
One delights in dwelling in the world and does not delight in dwelling in that which is non-worldly,
because the world possesses the fault of impermanence.
There are three kinds of worlds.
It is also as previously stated.
That which is not of the world is that wherein there is no place of great terror among any phenomena.
Furthermore, that which is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) is designated as "the mundane" (*loka*).
That upon which the two vehicles rely is designated as "non-mundane.
Therefore, it is said to be "fearful."
In the "Explanation of the Ten Epithets" within the "Chapter on the Sixteen Brahma-Conducts" of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*,
it says regarding the explanation of the epithet "Knower of the World":
"There are six kinds of worlds."

First, "world" (*loka*) refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), for the world consists of the five aggregates. Furthermore, "world" refers to the worlds of the lands in the ten directions, numbering incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*). Moreover, "world" refers to all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the sentient beings of the six elements (*ṣaḍ-dhātu*). Again, "world" refers to the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), which are like lotus flowers. Furthermore, "world" refers to the bodhisattvas, who also include the two vehicles. Finally, "world" is called the world of the five desires; since the causal dharmas are established separately, one should know that although six types are added by including the causal dharmas, [the term "world" encompasses them].
Nor do they exceed three;
for within the ten suchnesses (daśatathatā), the causal dharmas are contained.
Now, based on their specific meanings, each of the ten realms is opened up into three [categories].
Furthermore, the following ten kinds explain the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*).
These ten suchnesses are precisely the provisional and real aspects of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
and they are also the body of the vehicle.
It is also the essence of the Jewel.
Since the present object is that very essence, it must be clarified.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) of all phenomena is what is called the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena."
Since it is said that "all dharmas," the true aspect (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is itself the ten;
since it is said that "the true aspect," the ten are themselves the true aspect.
Therefore, my present interpretation does not accord with others.
If one does not encompass the phenomena within a single thought-moment by means of the ten realms, the inclusion of events will not be universal;
if one does not subsume the principle through the three truths, the integration of reality will not be complete;
and if one does not speak of the ten suchnesses, the causes and effects will not be fully prepared.
There is nothing within the three worlds— neither the environment nor its inhabitants—
that is not exhausted [by these ten aspects].
As for the term "ten suchnesses" (shí rú), this is because when Nanyue read the text, he took "rú" (suchness) as the final character of each phrase.
The Great Master of Tiantai reads the text according to its meaning in three ways.
First, he takes "thus" (tathatā) as the phrase; "thus" is emptiness.
Next, take "characteristics and nature" as a phrase;
the difference between characteristics and nature is the provisional.
Next, take "this" as a phrase.
In this regard, the reality of the Middle Way is itself the Middle,
because each and every realm is endowed with the three truths.
Although the meaning is thus, it is commonly observed that many [texts] form their phrases based on "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) and "nature" (*svabhāva*).
This accords with the verse which states: "Nature, characteristics, meaning, and so forth."
First, I shall explain the ten realms, the five aggregates, and the ten suchnesses. Within this,
I will first provide a general explanation,
followed by a detailed explanation.
First, by using the general meaning to crown the specific, the distinct meanings of the latter will become clearly visible.
In the initial explanation of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there are the dharma, the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the synthesis (*upanaya*).
Within the analogy, water and fire are used to illustrate their distinctness.
Because they can be grasped and distinguished, they are called "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*).
It is like a person's facial expression, which is termed a "characteristic" because it appears first.
As for the terms "prosperity" and "adversity":
The *Erya* says:
"Hsiu" means joy. The *Guangya* says: [it means to rest].
"Qing" (affirmation) signifies good; "Pi" (negation) signifies evil.

Regarding those such as Sun and Liu in the past:
they cited historical events to verify the signs previously manifested.
At the end of the Han dynasty, these three men went together to consult a physiognomist.
The physiognomist saw that Sun and Liu possessed the marks of those destined to rule the state;
he immediately informed them of this.
Lord Cao, however, was not noted by the physiognomist.
The physiognomist did not reach him, but pulled up his robes to show him.
Having seen him, the physiognomist raised his voice and wept bitterly.
"The world will stand like three鼎 (tripods), and the four seas will be divided into three parts."
"Tu" refers to the bitter herb.
By the end of the Later Han dynasty,
these three men indeed came to occupy the three regions.
Sun occupied Wu;
Liu occupied Shu;
Cao occupied Wei.
The two Han dynasties, preceding and following, together with the eighteen years of Wang Mang and the one year of Liu Xian,
total four hundred and twenty-six years.
At the end of the Later Han dynasty, during the reign of Emperor Xian, Dong Zhuo incited a rebellion.
He murdered the Empress Dowager and burned Luoyang.
The five planets lost their proper courses, and the five sacred peaks split asunder.
The earth quaked in the regions where the *tengu* spirits were prevalent;
white halos pierced the sun and crimson vapors penetrated the palace.
A single *hu* of grain was worth five million coins.
A bushel of beans cost two hundred thousand coins.
In the prefectures and counties, the various ministers were each reduced to starvation and death.
By the first year of Jian’an, Cao [Cao Cao] had become the Commandant of the Imperial Attendants (Sīlì xiàowèi).
Cao was originally a native of Pei.
His surname was Cao,
and his given name was Cao.
His courtesy name was Mengde.
He was a descendant of Cao Can of the Han dynasty.
From his youth, he was highly quick-witted and astute.
He possessed clever stratagems;
he delighted in flying hawks and running dogs, wandering about without restraint.
Yet, the people of the world did not consider him extraordinary.
Only He Yong of Nanyang and others found this strange.
It is unknown whether there was a separate account of a physiognomist in his original biography.
He Yong said to him:
In my observations of the scholars of the world, I have seen none like you.
If the world is about to fall into chaos, no one but a man of destiny can save it;
the one capable of bringing peace lies with you.
While serving as Commandant, he took charge of the affairs of the Minister of the Secretariat.
In the second year, Yuan Shao claimed the title of Son of Heaven;
in the eighth year, Cao [Cao Cao] was still the Governor of Jizhou.
In the thirteenth year, Cao [Cao Cao] became Chancellor.
In the eighteenth year, Cao styled himself Duke of Wei.
In the nineteenth year, Liu Bei and Liu Zhang took control of Yizhou.
Bei, whose courtesy name was Xu德 (Xu-de),
was a native of Zhu Jun.
Bei served the local government as if he were serving his father.
He was orphaned at a young age.
His mother made her living by selling sandals and working as a weaver for hire.
On a fence to the southeast corner of their house stood a mulberry tree.
It was over five *zhang* in height,
and its shape constantly appeared like a small carriage canopy when viewed from afar;
those who passed by marveled at it.
Someone remarked,
"This family will produce a person of noble station.
While [the child] was still young, he played beneath it, saying:
"I must ride in this carriage with its feathered canopy.
His son and grandson were startled and said, "Do not speak such reckless words; you will bring ruin upon our family!"
As he grew older, he took no pleasure in reading books;
he longed instead for hounds and horses,
and for the performance of music.
He wore beautiful garments;
he was seven chi and five cun tall,
with hands that reached below his knees.
He spoke little.
He was kind toward those of lower station.
His joy and anger were never manifested on his countenance.
This is the manifestation of his outward appearance.
In the twentieth year of Jian’an,
Cao [Cao Cao] killed the Empress and the Crown Prince.
In the twenty-first year, he styled himself the Lord of Wei.
In that same year, Liu Bei styled himself the Prince of Hanzhong.
Sun Chuan was unable to record these events in full detail.
The mutual concealment between Cao Gong and the others is like the eight realms;
the mutual manifestation between Sun and Liu is like the two realms.
Or, having already attained non-arising, their characteristics are manifested externally.
This is just like Maitreya,
whose prophecies are recorded both far and near.
Prophecies concerning the distant future are, for example, the records of the pigeon and the sparrow attaining Buddhahood.
In the "Chapter on the Dharma Master," I have bestowed predictions upon every single word and verse;
likewise for those such as Sadāparibhūta and others who are near to receiving their prediction.
As with Maitreya and the nine hundred and ninety-five Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa,

at the conclusion of the assemblies of various sutras, they receive the prediction of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) or even the stage of "one more birth" (ekajātipratibaddha), according to the two gates of the *Dharmapada* and the *Mūla*.
It is also like the four kinds of predictions in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*.
The Buddha told Resolute Mind (Dṛḍhamati):
"From this day forward, these evil Māras..."
"Gradually you shall attain the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and even achieve Buddhahood.
Mañjuśrī said to Māra, "The Tathāgata has already bestowed a prediction upon you.
Māra replied:
"My mind is impure; why has the Tathāgata bestowed a prediction upon me? [The Buddha replied:
"It is because the Buddha wishes to sever the doubts of all sentient beings."
He addressed Sthiramati, saying:
"There are four kinds of predictions (vyākaraṇa).
The first is the prediction for those who have not yet resolved their minds [for enlightenment]."
Some may transmigrate through the six realms of existence;
born among humans, they take delight in the Buddha-dharma and shall only after passing hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.
Having practiced the bodhisattva path for more than hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas,
and having even made offerings to Buddhas and transformed sentient beings,
all of which required passing through such kalpas, one shall attain bodhi.
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha,
"I now regard all living beings as the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"O Benevolent One, it is well said.
One should not recklessly attempt to measure sentient beings;
only the Tathāgata can truly measure them."
Second, the bestowal of a prediction upon the initial arousal of the mind:
this person has planted various roots of goodness over many kalpas;
they delight in the Great Dharma and possess a heart of compassion.
Because upon generating the mind of enlightenment, one immediately abides on the stage of non-retrogression, the Buddha grants the prediction (vyākaraṇa) to those who have so resolved.
Regarding the three secrets of the prediction, there are bodhisattvas who have not yet received such a prediction.
As they practice the six perfections, their merit becomes fully perfected.
The eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, all form this thought:
"When will this bodhisattva attain awakening?"
As for the number of disciples in this land during the kalpa,
the Buddha severed this doubt by immediately bestowing upon them their predictions of enlightenment;
the entire assembly came to know this.
This bodhisattva alone did not know [this].
Regarding the prediction of the fourfold patience toward the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*),
it was bestowed publicly in the midst of the great assembly.
Among the four types of predictions in the sūtras,
